analysis.one_liner: Forces pharmacy middlemen to disclose fees, bans spread pricing, and requires all drugmaker rebates to go to health plans.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee approved this PBM crackdown with bipartisan support in June 2023 and put it on the Senate calendar, but it never got a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that run drug benefits for employer health plans. This bill would force PBMs to tell employers in detail what drugs cost, how much they receive in rebates and fees from drugmakers, and how much they steer patients to pharmacies they own. It would ban 'spread pricing' — charging the health plan more for a drug than the pharmacy was paid — and require PBMs to hand over 100% of drugmaker rebates to the plan, with fines of $10,000 a day for violations. The Senate health committee approved it with bipartisan support, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people with employer health coverage, who pay part of their drug costs out of pocket and whose premiums reflect what plans spend on drugs. Employers who sponsor health plans also gain new visibility and audit rights, and community pharmacies gain from the ban on being paid less than the plan is charged.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with job-based coverage and pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Requires PBMs to report annually to health plan sponsors on drug costs, the rebates and fees they receive from drugmakers, total gross versus net spending, and payments to brokers and consultants who steered the plan's business to them [S2][S3].
Prohibits spread pricing — a PBM charging the health plan, or the plan charging patients, more for a drug than the pharmacy was paid [S2][S3].
Requires PBMs, insurers, and third-party administrators to remit 100% of manufacturer rebates, fees, and discounts to the health plan within 90 days, with audit rights for plan sponsors [S2][S3].

Requires six-month supplementary reports on prescriptions dispensed by pharmacies that the PBM or insurer owns, including what those pharmacies charged versus what independent pharmacies in the same network charged for the same drug [S2][S3].
Enforces the rules with civil penalties of $10,000 per day for failing to disclose, and up to $100,000 per item of knowingly false information [S3].
Bars employers from firing or discriminating against an employee based on their drug-spending information reported under the bill [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them, who lose spread-pricing income and rebate 'float,' and drugmakers whose rebate arrangements would be exposed to employer scrutiny. Some compliance costs could flow into premiums or PBM fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy middlemen and their insurer owners

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap what PBMs can charge; it allows them to keep collecting fees for 'bona fide services' as long as those fees are transparent, so PBMs could reprice rather than shrink their take [S3].

The most detailed reporting requirements apply to large-employer plans (50 or more employees); plans of small employers get a lighter version, and health insurers' detailed reports are largely opt-in unless the plan sponsor demands them [S3].
PBMs may place 'reasonable restrictions' on public disclosure of the reports, so much of the data would go to employers and regulators rather than to the public [S3].
Compliance costs fall on PBMs, insurers, and plan administrators, and honest supporters acknowledge that some of that cost could be passed to plan sponsors and, through premiums, to workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: workers and employers have had no way to see where their drug dollars went, and this bill would open the books and stop two of the most criticized practices — spread pricing and rebate retention. Its limits are that it relies on transparency rather than price caps, exempts the smallest employers from full reporting, and lets much of the information stay out of public view. It would not by itself lower drug list prices, but it targets a middleman layer that both parties have blamed for opaque costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it with bipartisan backing and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but no floor vote ever happened before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, with original cosponsors including Senators Cassidy, Murray, Marshall, and Braun, and it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S3][S5].

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on May 11, 2023, and reported it on June 22, 2023 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, meaning the committee replaced the original text with its own version [S5].
The reported bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 113) on June 22, 2023, where it sat without ever coming to a vote [S5].

The details described here reflect the bill as introduced and summarized by the Congressional Research Service; the committee's substitute version was never voted on by the full Senate, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S2][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pharmacy benefit manager industry and the insurers that own them came out ahead: with no floor vote ever scheduled, spread pricing, retained rebates, and limited disclosure of their fees continued unchanged through the end of the Congress. Employers and pharmacies that wanted transparency also lost out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurers

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (I-VT), Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee that approved and reported it, and placed the reported bill on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-LA), ranking member of the Senate HELP Committee

for.name: Community pharmacies and pharmacist groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed PBM reform, including spread-pricing bans, as a fix for pharmacies being reimbursed below what plans are charged.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the reported bill, which sat on the Senate calendar, up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)

sides.party_line_note: An independent senator introduced the bill with three Republican and one Democratic cosponsors, and a Senate committee with members of both parties reported it favorably; the bill died for lack of floor time, not party opposition on the record.

industries.note: PBMs earn money on the gap between what a plan is charged and what a pharmacy is paid (spread pricing) and by keeping a share of drugmaker rebates. The bill bans spread pricing, requires full rebate pass-through, and exposes their fees, threatening a major revenue model; the public pays for that model through higher plan and out-of-pocket drug costs.

The spread-pricing ban stops the practice of paying a pharmacy less than the plan or patient is charged for the same drug, and owned-pharmacy reporting would reveal when a PBM's own pharmacies are favored. Independent pharmacies have been closing under PBM reimbursement pressure.

industries.industry: Health insurers with PBM affiliates (CVS/Aetna, Cigna, UnitedHealth)
industries.note: The bill imposes reporting and rebate-pass-through duties on insurers and third-party administrators and requires disclosure of dispensing by PBM- and insurer-owned pharmacies, pressing on the vertically integrated model through which these companies capture drug-benefit revenue. Their gain comes from that integration, which this bill would make visible and less profitable.

Plan sponsors get detailed annual and semiannual reports, full rebate remittance within 90 days, and audit rights over rebate contracts — tools to negotiate and verify what they are paying for employee drug benefits.

Rebates, fees, and discounts the manufacturers pay would have to be remitted in full to plans and disclosed to employers, exposing rebate-driven pricing, but the bill does not cap drug prices itself and would still allow manufacturer copay-assistance programs, which the reports would count.
